title: Connected home device — firmware, companion app and cloud backend
description: A consumer IoT product: an embedded device with field-updatable firmware, a companion mobile app used to provision and control it, and a cloud backend the device phones home to for telemetry and remote commands. Seeded as a starting template for the IoT / embedded system archetype, covering the device, the app, the backend and physical access to the unit itself.

risks.title: Malicious firmware causes unsafe device behaviour
risks.description: Tampered firmware makes the device act outside its safe operating envelope (for example overriding a thermal cutoff or a physical lock state), leading to a safety incident and a mandatory field recall of the affected product line.

risks.title: Devices recruited into a botnet
risks.description: A large fraction of the installed base is compromised and used for outbound DDoS or spam traffic, resulting in ISP-level blacklisting of the vendor's cloud ranges, a mandatory patch campaign, and penalty clauses in retail-partner contracts for shipping vulnerable units.

risks.title: Customer PII exposed via companion app or cloud backend
risks.description: An attacker obtains customer account details, device location history and usage patterns, either by extracting credentials from the companion app or by pulling records directly from the cloud backend, triggering breach-notification duties and regulator attention.

risks.title: Mass unauthorized control of customer devices via the cloud API
risks.description: An attacker exploits authorization flaws in the backend API to enumerate and take over many customer accounts at once, then issues commands to their devices at scale — unlocking, disabling, or otherwise overriding safety-relevant settings — for extortion or as a public demonstration of the product's insecurity.

attacks.title: Malicious firmware pushed via an unauthenticated update channel
attacks.description: The device fetches firmware images over an unencrypted connection with no signature verification, letting a network-position attacker or a spoofed update server deliver an attacker-controlled image that the device installs without question.

references.title: Download of Code Without Integrity Check

attacks.title: Login using hardcoded or default device credentials
attacks.description: A factory-set username and password, identical across the entire product line and either baked into the firmware or documented in a public manual, gives an attacker shell or administrative access to any unit they can reach.

attacks.title: Exploitation of the device cloud backend API
attacks.description: Missing per-device authorization checks on the backend API let an authenticated attacker change a device identifier in a request and act on a unit they do not own, from reading its telemetry to issuing it commands.

attacks.title: Extraction of credentials from the companion mobile app
attacks.description: The companion app writes the account session token and the Wi-Fi credentials used to provision the device to plaintext local storage, recoverable by another app on the same phone, from a phone backup, or from a lost or resold handset.

attacks.title: Firmware extraction via an exposed physical debug port
attacks.description: An accessible UART or JTAG header on the production circuit board lets anyone with brief physical access to a purchased or stolen unit dump the running firmware image and any secrets embedded in it, or flash a modified image directly onto the board.

attacks.title: Replay and spoofing of device telemetry and commands
attacks.description: Without a freshness or sequence check on messages, a captured telemetry report or command can be recorded and replayed later, or a forged command can be injected onto the channel as if it came from the legitimate app.

defences.title: Cryptographically signed firmware with mandatory verification
defences.description: Every firmware image is signed by the manufacturer's build pipeline, and the bootloader refuses to flash or boot an image whose signature does not verify against the embedded manufacturer key.

attack-unauth-firmware-update.rationale: An unsigned or tampered image is rejected outright by the bootloader; only a compromise of the signing key itself, which is held offline, would defeat this.

defences.title: TLS with certificate pinning for all device-to-cloud traffic
defences.description: Firmware downloads, telemetry uploads and command delivery all move to TLS 1.2+, with the device pinning the backend's certificate and refusing to talk to any endpoint presenting an unpinned or self-signed certificate.

attack-unauth-firmware-update.rationale: Certificate pinning closes off the network-position and spoofed-update-server routes that this attack relies on, independent of the signature check itself.

attack-insecure-cloud-api.rationale: Encrypting the channel stops a passive observer from harvesting session tokens in transit, but does nothing about the missing authorization check that this attack actually exploits, hence the modest rating.

attack-telemetry-command-spoofing.rationale: TLS session framing makes a naively captured-and-replayed message harder to reuse verbatim, though it does not add an explicit freshness check on its own.

defences.title: Unique per-device credentials generated at provisioning
defences.description: Each unit is provisioned at the factory with a randomly generated, device-unique administrative password and API key, printed on a removable label, replacing the single credential shared across the whole product line.

attack-hardcoded-credentials.rationale: Compromising one unit's credential no longer yields access to any other unit; only reduces the impact of a factory-database leak rather than the per-device brute-force route, hence short of full coverage.

defences.title: Secure boot and disabled debug ports on production units
defences.description: The JTAG and UART headers are electrically fused off after factory test, and a secure boot chain refuses to execute an unsigned image even if an attacker manages to reflash the chip directly through the remaining physical interfaces.

attack-physical-debug-port.rationale: Removes the two most direct physical extraction paths at once; a sufficiently resourced attacker with chip-level lab equipment is still out of scope for this control.

defences.title: Platform keystore storage for companion app secrets
defences.description: The companion app moves the account session token and the Wi-Fi credentials used during provisioning out of plaintext local storage and into the operating system's keystore or keychain, encrypted at rest and scoped to the app.

attack-companion-app-insecure-storage.rationale: Keystore-backed secrets are no longer readable by another app or a simple filesystem dump; a rooted or jailbroken phone in the attacker's possession can still extract them, hence short of full coverage.

defences.title: Per-device authorization checks and rate limiting on the cloud API
defences.description: Every API call is checked against the caller's own recorded device ownership before it is allowed to touch a device record, and request rates are capped per account to slow down enumeration attempts that try to find valid device identifiers.

attack-insecure-cloud-api.rationale: Directly closes the missing-authorization gap this attack depends on; the remaining fraction accounts for an attacker who compromises a legitimately owned device's own credentials instead.

attack-telemetry-command-spoofing.rationale: Rate limiting makes a bulk replay campaign harder to run unnoticed, but does not add a per-message freshness check, so a low-volume targeted replay still gets through.

defences.title: Legacy shared factory secret authentication (deprecated)
defences.description: The original authentication scheme, in which every unit in a product line embedded the same factory secret, now superseded by the per-device credential rollout and kept only as a reference point for units still in the field.

attack-hardcoded-credentials.rationale: Offered no meaningful resistance once the shared secret leaked once, which is exactly what happened and is why the scheme was retired.

defences.title: Product liability insurance and limitation-of-liability clause
defences.description: An annual liability policy covering recall and safety-incident response costs, combined with a limitation-of-liability clause in the end-user terms of use that caps claims for consequential damages arising from a security incident.

attack-unauth-firmware-update.rationale: Policy sub-limits and the deductible mean roughly a third of the loss on an incident reached through this path is reimbursed or capped on average.

attack-insecure-cloud-api.rationale: Lower coverage than the firmware path: the policy excludes losses traced to a known, unpatched authorization flaw once it has been formally reported internally, which this finding already has been.
